readings: Join Invoices to Orders and to Customers. For each customer gender (NULL gender is its own group), count the DISTINCT orders that have at least one invoice. Take the plain average of these per-gender counts. Keep only genders whose count is strictly above that average. Return one row with the average count of those genders and the average amount by which their counts exceed the per-gender average.

Join Invoices to Orders and to Customers. For each customer gender (NULL gender is its own group), count the invoice records (each invoice counts once, so an order with several invoices is counted several times). Take the plain average of these per-gender counts. Keep only genders whose count is strictly above that average. Return one row with the average count of those genders and the average amount by which their counts exceed the per-gender average.
queries:
WITH g AS (
  SELECT c.gender AS gender, COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS cnt
  FROM Invoices i
  JOIN Orders o ON i.order_id = o.order_id
  JOIN Customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
  GROUP BY c.gender
),
a AS (
  SELECT AVG(cnt) AS avg_cnt FROM g
)
SELECT AVG(g.cnt) AS average_count,
       AVG(g.cnt - a.avg_cnt) AS average_excess
FROM g, a
WHERE g.cnt > a.avg_cnt;
WITH g AS (
  SELECT c.gender AS gender, COUNT(*) AS cnt
  FROM Invoices i
  JOIN Orders o ON i.order_id = o.order_id
  JOIN Customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
  GROUP BY c.gender
),
a AS (
  SELECT AVG(cnt) AS avg_cnt FROM g
)
SELECT AVG(g.cnt) AS avg_count, AVG(g.cnt - a.avg_cnt) AS avg_excess
FROM g, a
WHERE g.cnt > a.avg_cnt;
